title: Were there any movies with text dialogue that synched on screen as the characters talking during the silent era similar to modern subtitles?

commenti.body:
I don't know of any although I've actually considered doing this myself with some shorts to see how it works. Of course, a lot of title cards in silent films aren't actually the dialogue, but are establishing the setting or commenting on the action.

One notable exception is Charlie Chaplin's Gold Rush. In the 1930s he released a new version with all the titles removed and he narrates the story instead. I like it better and it's much shorter.

This site (https://the-artifice.com/subtitling-cinema-history/) has a ton of examples of subtitles (not intertitles) in silent movies. It’s surprisingly thorough. One of the first examples is College Chums from 2907 which can be found here: https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=30bqiFAX3PA. The scene with the telephone uses a peculiar form of subtitles.

I did some poking around and a ton of articles said the first device that put subtitles *under* the movie was patented by MN Tropp in 1909. However, this seems to be a hoax as most of the articles used the same wording and I couldn’t find the patent record. Nevertheless, there are earlier examples of subtitle use in the article I provided. I originally wrote a long comment that went over the highlights from the article but I accidentally deleted it - oh well.

The new version *The Gold Rush* is dated to 1942 according to Wikipedia. I was curious about when it appeared, because I have seen *Modern Times* claimed as the first time that the public ever heard Chaplin’s voice (and then he didn’t even speak but sing).
Ah, I wasn't sure when it was released. I just knew it was the sound era.

Intertitles were probably technically much easier to do than subtitles. And they were "good enough".


I would also like to point out that films were shown globally, and I would assume that intertitles could be cut and replaced with other languages; subtitles might have made things more difficult.
